claim: Drosophila melanogaster has approximately 1100 descending neurons (DNs).
source: In the fly, Drosophila melanogaster, this is coordinated by a population of ~ 1100 descending neurons (DNs).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the approximate number of DNs in the abstract.

claim: Activating only a few DNs is sufficient to drive complex behaviors like walking and grooming.
source: Activating only a few DNs is known to be sufficient to drive complex behaviors like walking and grooming.
evidence: The abstract states this as known information, implying citation to prior work.

claim: The largest fraction of recorded DNs encode walking.
source: We found that the largest fraction of recorded DNs encode walking while fewer are active during head grooming and resting.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Fewer DNs are active during head grooming compared to walking.
source: We found that the largest fraction of recorded DNs encode walking while fewer are active during head grooming and resting.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: A large fraction of walk-encoding DNs encode turning.
source: A large fraction of walk-encoding DNs encode turning and far fewer weakly encode speed.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Far fewer walk-encoding DNs weakly encode speed.
source: A large fraction of walk-encoding DNs encode turning and far fewer weakly encode speed.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Odor context does not determine which behavior-encoding DNs are recruited.
source: Although odor context does not determine which behavior-encoding DNs are recruited, a few DNs encode odors rather than behaviors.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: A few DNs encode odors rather than behaviors.
source: Although odor context does not determine which behavior-encoding DNs are recruited, a few DNs encode odors rather than behaviors.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: DN axons impinge upon local circuits including central pattern generators (CPGs) that transform DN directives into specific limb or body part movements.
source: There, DN axons impinge upon local circuits including central pattern generators (CPGs) that transform DN directives into specific limb or body part movements (Bouvier et al., 2015; Capelli et al., 2017; Caggiano et al., 2018; Orger et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: DNs make up only about 1% of brain neurons.
source: Because DNs make up only about 1% of brain neurons, DN population activity represents a critical information bottleneck: high-dimensional brain dynamics must be compressed into low-dimensional commands that efficiently interface with and are read out by motor circuits.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the introduction.

claim: Drosophila are thought to have between ~350 and ~500 pairs of DNs.
source: Drosophila are thought to have between ~350 (Namiki et al., 2018) and ~500 (Hsu and Bhandawat, 2016) pairs of DNs.
evidence: This statement is supported by two citations providing different estimates.

claim: Artificial activation of DN pairs is sufficient to drive complex behaviors including escape (giant fiber neurons, 'GF').
source: These studies have demonstrated that artificial activation of DN pairs is sufficient to drive complex behaviors including escape (Lima and Miesenböck, 2005) (giant fiber neurons, 'GF'), antennal grooming (Hampel et al., 2015)(antennal descending neurons, 'aDN'), backward walking (Bidaye et al., 2014) (moonwalker descending neurons, 'MDN'), forward walking (Bidaye et al., 2020) (DNp09), and landing (Ache et al., 2019a) (DNp10 and DNp07).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lima and Miesenböck, 2005.

claim: Artificial activation of DN pairs is sufficient to drive antennal grooming (antennal descending neurons, 'aDN').
source: These studies have demonstrated that artificial activation of DN pairs is sufficient to drive complex behaviors including escape (Lima and Miesenböck, 2005) (giant fiber neurons, 'GF'), antennal grooming (Hampel et al., 2015)(antennal descending neurons, 'aDN'), backward walking (Bidaye et al., 2014) (moonwalker descending neurons, 'MDN'), forward walking (Bidaye et al., 2020) (DNp09), and landing (Ache et al., 2019a) (DNp10 and DNp07).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hampel et al., 2015.

claim: Artificial activation of DN pairs is sufficient to drive backward walking (moonwalker descending neurons, 'MDN').
source: These studies have demonstrated that artificial activation of DN pairs is sufficient to drive complex behaviors including escape (Lima and Miesenböck, 2005) (giant fiber neurons, 'GF'), antennal grooming (Hampel et al., 2015)(antennal descending neurons, 'aDN'), backward walking (Bidaye et al., 2014) (moonwalker descending neurons, 'MDN'), forward walking (Bidaye et al., 2020) (DNp09), and landing (Ache et al., 2019a) (DNp10 and DNp07).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bidaye et al., 2014.

claim: Artificial activation of DN pairs is sufficient to drive forward walking (DNp09).
source: These studies have demonstrated that artificial activation of DN pairs is sufficient to drive complex behaviors including escape (Lima and Miesenböck, 2005) (giant fiber neurons, 'GF'), antennal grooming (Hampel et al., 2015)(antennal descending neurons, 'aDN'), backward walking (Bidaye et al., 2014) (moonwalker descending neurons, 'MDN'), forward walking (Bidaye et al., 2020) (DNp09), and landing (Ache et al., 2019a) (DNp10 and DNp07).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bidaye et al., 2020.

claim: Artificial activation of DN pairs is sufficient to drive landing (DNp10 and DNp07).
source: These studies have demonstrated that artificial activation of DN pairs is sufficient to drive complex behaviors including escape (Lima and Miesenböck, 2005) (giant fiber neurons, 'GF'), antennal grooming (Hampel et al., 2015)(antennal descending neurons, 'aDN'), backward walking (Bidaye et al., 2014) (moonwalker descending neurons, 'MDN'), forward walking (Bidaye et al., 2020) (DNp09), and landing (Ache et al., 2019a) (DNp10 and DNp07).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ache et al., 2019a.

claim: Optogenetic activation of most DNs drives only small changes in locomotor and grooming behaviors.
source: Notably, a behavioral screen revealed that optogenetic activation of most DNs drives only small changes in locomotor and grooming behaviors (Cande, 2018) rather than a large variety of distinct actions as might be expected if each DN was a command-like neuron.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cande, 2018.

claim: Changes in the firing rates of some DNs correlate with walking speed and turning.
source: In line with having a role in behavioral modulation, studies in crickets and locusts have demonstrated that changes in the firing rates of some DNs (Böhm and Schildberger, 1992; Zorović and Hedwig, 2011) correlate with walking speed and turning (Heinrich, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies in crickets and locusts.

claim: DNa02 activity is observed in response to fictive odors in immobile flies.
source: For example, in addition to discovering DNs that are active during steering, one recent study also observed DNa02 activity in response to fictive odors in immobile flies (Rayshubskiy, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rayshubskiy, 2020.

claim: DNp07 activity has been observed in response to visual stimulation in nonflying flies.
source: DNp07 activity has also been observed in response to visual stimulation in nonflying flies (Ache et al., 2019a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ache et al., 2019a.

claim: The driver line used restricts expression to the supraesophageal zone of the brain.
source: First, we restricted the expression of GCaMP6s (a fluorescent indicator of neural activity; Chen et al., 2013) and tdTomato (an anatomical fiduciary) to the supraesophageal zone of the brain (Asahina et al., 2014) (;otd-nls:FLPo; R57C10-GAL4, tub>GAL80>).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by a citation.

claim: The driver line lacks expression in the subesophageal zone (SEZ).
source: Thus, although our driver line lacks expression in the subesophageal zone (SEZ) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c)—a brain region known to house at least 41 DNs (Sterne et al., 2021; Namiki et al., 2018) some of which can drive grooming (Guo et al., 2022) (DNg11, DNg12)—we could still capture the activities of a large population of DNs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure reference and citations.

claim: The subesophageal zone (SEZ) is known to house at least 41 DNs.
source: Thus, although our driver line lacks expression in the subesophageal zone (SEZ) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c)—a brain region known to house at least 41 DNs (Sterne et al., 2021; Namiki et al., 2018) some of which can drive grooming (Guo et al., 2022) (DNg11, DNg12)—we could still capture the activities of a large population of DNs.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sterne et al., 2021 and Namiki et al., 2018.

claim: Some DNs in the SEZ can drive grooming (DNg11, DNg12).
source: Thus, although our driver line lacks expression in the subesophageal zone (SEZ) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c)—a brain region known to house at least 41 DNs (Sterne et al., 2021; Namiki et al., 2018) some of which can drive grooming (Guo et al., 2022) (DNg11, DNg12)—we could still capture the activities of a large population of DNs.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2022.

claim: ACV is an attractive odorant.
source: To test the context-dependence and sensory feedback encoding of DNs, we built an olfactometer that could sequentially present humidified air and one of two odors: ACV (an attractive odorant; Semmelhack and Wang, 2009) or MSC (a putatively aversive odorant; Mohamed et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Semmelhack and Wang, 2009.

claim: MSC is a putatively aversive odorant.
source: To test the context-dependence and sensory feedback encoding of DNs, we built an olfactometer that could sequentially present humidified air and one of two odors: ACV (an attractive odorant; Semmelhack and Wang, 2009) or MSC (a putatively aversive odorant; Mohamed et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mohamed et al., 2019.

claim: Approximately 60% of DNs encode walking.
source: The largest fraction (~60%) of DNs encode walking.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2c.

claim: Approximately 15% of DNs encode head grooming.
source: The second largest group of DNs encode head grooming (~15%).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2c.

claim: Only a very small fraction of DNs encode resting.
source: Only a very small fraction of DNs encode resting and no neurons encode front leg rubbing or posterior movements (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2c.

claim: No neurons encode front leg rubbing or posterior movements.
source: Only a very small fraction of DNs encode resting and no neurons encode front leg rubbing or posterior movements (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2c.

claim: DNs encoding walking also encoded posterior movements.
source: As well, although none of the DNs best explained posterior movements and front leg rubbing out of all behaviors we observed that DNs encoding walking also encoded posterior movements.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: DNs encoding head grooming also encoded front leg rubbing.
source: Similarly, DNs encoding head grooming also encoded front leg rubbing (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: DNs predominantly encode walking rather than posterior movements.
source: These analyses confirmed that DNs predominantly encode walking rather than posterior movements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) and head grooming rather than front leg rubbing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: DNs predominantly encode head grooming rather than front leg rubbing.
source: These analyses confirmed that DNs predominantly encode walking rather than posterior movements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) and head grooming rather than front leg rubbing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Joint angles can only very marginally improve the prediction of neural activity beyond simply using behavior regressors.
source: We found that joint angles can only very marginally improve the prediction of neural activity beyond simply using behavior regressors (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: DN populations largely encode high-level behaviors suggesting that they delegate low-level kinematic control to downstream circuits in the VNC.
source: Thus, DN populations largely encode high-level behaviors suggesting that they delegate low-level kinematic control to downstream circuits in the VNC.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the finding that joint angles do not improve neural activity prediction.

claim: DNs encoding walking are spread throughout the dorsal connective.
source: We found that DNs encoding walking are spread throughout the dorsal connective (Figure 2e, g and h).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2e, g, and h.

claim: Head groom-encoding DNs are predominantly in the ventral connective.
source: On the other hand, head groom-encoding DNs are predominantly in the ventral connective (Figure 2g and i) including two prominent pairs—lateral and medial-ventral (Figure 2e, white arrowheads)—whose activities explain the largest amount of variance in head grooming across animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2g and i.

claim: Two prominent pairs of head groom-encoding DNs—lateral and medial-ventral—explain the largest amount of variance in head grooming across animals.
source: On the other hand, head groom-encoding DNs are predominantly in the ventral connective (Figure 2g and i) including two prominent pairs—lateral and medial-ventral (Figure 2e, white arrowheads)—whose activities explain the largest amount of variance in head grooming across animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Rest-encoding DNs were located medially, close to the giant fibers, as well as in the lateral extremities of the connective.
source: These were located medially, close to the giant fibers, as well as in the lateral extremities of the connective (Figure 2e, olive circles).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2e.

claim: The first two PCs can explain upwards of 60% of the variance in DN population activity during walking.
source: We found that the first two PCs can explain upwards of 60% of the variance in DN population activity during walking (Figure 2j, Figure 2—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2j and Figure 2—figure supplement 4a.

claim: 2D trajectories of DN activity during individual walking bouts move primarily along two directions.
source: Visualizing 2D trajectories (PC 1 and PC 2 subspace) of DN activity during individual walking bouts revealed that they move primarily along two directions (Figure 2k, Figure 2—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2k and Figure 2—figure supplement 4b.

claim: DNs with the largest PC loadings are spatially segregated on opposite sides of the connective.
source: Consistently, also in flies with a less clear divergence in neural trajectories, we found subsets of DNs whose activities correspond to one of these two directions. By examining the positions of their axons we observed that they are spatially segregated on opposite sides of the connective (Figure 2—figure supplement 4d, cyan arrowheads).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4d.

claim: Neural activity could explain a great deal of variance in turning and, to a lesser extent, speed.
source: Neural activity could explain a great deal of variance in turning and, to a lesser extent, speed.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3a.

claim: Neural activity can uniquely explain turning to a greater extent (~60%) than it can explain walking speed (~30%).
source: In this manner, we confirmed that neural activity can uniquely explain turning to a greater extent (~60%) than it can explain walking speed (~30%) (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3b.

claim: Among DNs that encode walking, specific DNs strongly explain right or left turning.
source: Among DNs that encode walking, we found specific DNs that strongly explain right or left turning.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3c.

claim: A more distributed set of DNs weakly encode walking speed.
source: By contrast, a more distributed set of DNs weakly encode walking speed (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Across animals some walk-encoding DNs also strongly encoded turning.
source: This was also reflected in the amount of variance explained: across animals some walk-encoding DNs also strongly encoded turning (Figure 3e) whereas these DNs only encoded a tiny fraction of the variance in walking speed (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3e.

claim: Walk-encoding DNs only encoded a tiny fraction of the variance in walking speed.
source: This was also reflected in the amount of variance explained: across animals some walk-encoding DNs also strongly encoded turning (Figure 3e) whereas these DNs only encoded a tiny fraction of the variance in walking speed (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3f.

claim: There is both ipsi- and contralateral turn-encoding DNs on both sides of the connective but a clear ipsilateral enrichment.
source: We found both ipsi- and contralateral turn-encoding DNs on both sides of the connective (Figure 3g, Figure 3—figure supplement 2c) but a clear ipsilateral enrichment (Figure 3h, Figure 3—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3g, h and Figure 3—figure supplement 2c, d.

claim: Many of the DNs encoding turning had high PC loading.
source: Many of the DNs encoding turning had high PC loading (Figure 2—figure supplement 4d) revealing that turning contributes heavily to the variance in DN population dynamics during walking.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4d.

claim: Turning contributes heavily to the variance in DN population dynamics during walking.
source: Many of the DNs encoding turning had high PC loading (Figure 2—figure supplement 4d) revealing that turning contributes heavily to the variance in DN population dynamics during walking.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the finding that turn-encoding DNs have high PC loading.

claim: DNs encoding walking speed were more homogeneously distributed across the connective with no clear spatial enrichment.
source: By contrast, DNs encoding walking speed were more homogeneously distributed across the connective with no clear spatial enrichment (Figure 3i and j, Figure 3—figure supplement 2e and f).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3i, j and Figure 3—figure supplement 2e, f.

claim: An attractive odor, ACV, decreases resting and increases walking.
source: The possibility of recruiting separate pools of DNs for walking is supported by the observation that an attractive odor, ACV, decreases resting and increases walking (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), increases forward walking speed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), and reduces turning (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: ACV increases forward walking speed.
source: The possibility of recruiting separate pools of DNs for walking is supported by the observation that an attractive odor, ACV, decreases resting and increases walking (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), increases forward walking speed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), and reduces turning (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: ACV reduces turning.
source: The possibility of recruiting separate pools of DNs for walking is supported by the observation that an attractive odor, ACV, decreases resting and increases walking (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), increases forward walking speed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), and reduces turning (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: Largely the same DNs were highly predictive of walking irrespective of olfactory context.
source: We found that largely the same DNs were highly predictive of walking (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a) and head grooming (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b) irrespective of olfactory context.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Largely the same DNs were highly predictive of head grooming irrespective of olfactory context.
source: We found that largely the same DNs were highly predictive of walking (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a) and head grooming (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b) irrespective of olfactory context.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Only a very small fraction of DNs were differentially recruited during odor presentation.
source: Only a very small fraction of DNs were differentially recruited during odor presentation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a and b, black asterisks, two-sided Mann–Whitney U-test on cross-validation folds).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a and b.

claim: The activity of a few DNs could be uniquely explained by the presence of an odor.
source: We found that the activity of a few DNs could be uniquely explained by each of the odors (Figure 4b, asterisks).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4b.

claim: Clear activity peaks coincided with the presence of MSC.
source: In these neurons, clear activity peaks coincided with the presence of MSC (Figure 4c) or ACV (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4c.

claim: Clear activity peaks coincided with the presence of ACV.
source: In these neurons, clear activity peaks coincided with the presence of MSC (Figure 4c) or ACV (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4d.

claim: There appears to be no overlap between the DNs encoding MSC or ACV within individual animals.
source: Notably, there appears to be no overlap between the DNs encoding MSC or ACV within individual animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: MSC encoding neurons were found dorsally on the lateral sides of the giant fibers in the connective.
source: MSC encoding neurons were found dorsally on the lateral sides of the giant fibers in the connective while ACV encoding neurons were more broadly dispersed (Figure 4e and f).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4e and f.

claim: ACV encoding neurons were more broadly dispersed.
source: MSC encoding neurons were found dorsally on the lateral sides of the giant fibers in the connective while ACV encoding neurons were more broadly dispersed (Figure 4e and f).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4e and f.

claim: A large pair of ventral neurons sometimes exhibited asymmetric activity when flies appeared to touch one rather than both antennae.
source: Specifically, while analyzing head grooming DNs we noticed a large pair of ventral neurons (Figure 5a) that sometimes exhibited asymmetric activity (Figure 5b, gray arrowheads) when flies appeared to touch one rather than both antennae (Video 5).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5a, b and Video 5.

claim: Occasional asymmetries in antennal collisions coincided with asymmetric activity in corresponding neural data.
source: By detecting leg-antennal collisions as a proxy for antenna deflection, we found that occasional asymmetries (Figure 5d) did coincide with asymmetric activity in corresponding neural data (Figure 5b, purple traces).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5b and d.

claim: R65D11-GAL4 neurons encode sensory signals—antennal deflection—rather than behavior.
source: We measured an increase in the activity of both DNs upon puff stimulation (Figure 5g and h) suggesting that, like the neurons recorded in DN populations, R65D11 neurons also encode sensory signals—antennal deflection—rather than behavior.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5g and h.

claim: R65D11 DNs have a striking morphological similarity to DNx01 neurons.
source: Close examination of these neurites in the brain (Figure 5j) and VNC (Figure 5k) revealed a striking resemblance to the reported structure of DNx01 neurons (Namiki et al., 2018) with cell bodies outside of the brain—putatively in the antennae and enabling antennal mechanosensing.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5j and k and a citation.

claim: DNx01 neurons have cell bodies outside of the brain—putatively in the antennae and enabling antennal mechanosensing.
source: Close examination of these neurites in the brain (Figure 5j) and VNC (Figure 5k) revealed a striking resemblance to the reported structure of DNx01 neurons (Namiki et al., 2018) with cell bodies outside of the brain—putatively in the antennae and enabling antennal mechanosensing.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5j and k and a citation.

claim: Most recorded DNs encode walking.
source: Using this approach we found that most recorded DNs encode walking.
evidence: This is a summary finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: A smaller number of DNs are active during head grooming and resting.
source: A smaller number are active during head grooming and resting.
evidence: This is a summary finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: Subsets of walk-encoding DNs were strongly active during turning and were at higher density on the ipsilateral half of the cervical connective with respect to turn direction.
source: Subsets of walk-encoding DNs were also strongly active during turning: they were at higher density on the ipsilateral half of the cervical connective with respect to turn direction.
evidence: This is a summary finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: DNs distributed throughout the connective very weakly encoded walking speed.
source: By contrast, DNs distributed throughout the connective very weakly encoded walking speed.
evidence: This is a summary finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: The encoding of walking by large numbers of DNs supports the notion that the brain tightly regulates locomotion.
source: The encoding—and presumptive control—of walking by large numbers of DNs supports the notion that the brain tightly regulates locomotion.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Discussion.

claim: Head grooming is encoded by far fewer neurons in our dataset.
source: In contrast to walking, head grooming is encoded by far fewer neurons in our dataset.
evidence: This is a summary finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: Grooming limb movements may rely more heavily on controllers within the VNC.
source: This may be because grooming limb movements are more stereotyped and thus may rely more heavily on controllers within the VNC (a notion that is supported by the ability of headless flies to perform spontaneous grooming; Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Headless flies can perform spontaneous grooming.
source: This may be because grooming limb movements are more stereotyped and thus may rely more heavily on controllers within the VNC (a notion that is supported by the ability of headless flies to perform spontaneous grooming; Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Harris et al., 2015.

claim: Brain-wide activity occurs during walking but not during other behaviors.
source: Other studies have also shown brain-wide activity during walking but not during other behaviors (Aimon et al., 2019; Schaffer et al., 2021; Brezovec et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: Many ascending neurons (ANs) have been shown to encode walking.
source: Interestingly, many ascending neurons (ANs) have also been shown to encode walking (Chen, 2022; Fujiwara et al., 2022) with a large fraction projecting to the gnathal ganglia (GNG), a brain region that is also heavily innervated by DNs (Namiki et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Chen, 2022 and Fujiwara et al., 2022.

claim: A large fraction of ANs project to the gnathal ganglia (GNG), a brain region that is also heavily innervated by DNs.
source: Interestingly, many ascending neurons (ANs) have also been shown to encode walking (Chen, 2022; Fujiwara et al., 2022) with a large fraction projecting to the gnathal ganglia (GNG), a brain region that is also heavily innervated by DNs (Namiki et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Optogenetic activation of a large variety of DNs elicits only a small set of stereotyped behaviors.
source: This notion is supported by studies showing that optogenetic activation of a large variety of DNs elicits only a small set of stereotyped behaviors (Cande, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cande, 2018.

claim: The perception of a fictive odor modulates the activity of specific DNs involved in steering in immobile flies.
source: A nonbehavioral role for DNs has also been suggested by previous studies showing that the perception of a fictive odor modulates the activity of specific DNs involved in steering in immobile flies (Rayshubskiy, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rayshubskiy, 2020.

claim: The two odors presented—ACV and MSC—were encoded by distinct DNs.
source: Notably, the two odors we presented—ACV and MSC—were encoded by distinct DNs.
evidence: This is a summary finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: DNx01s may have a role beyond feedback control during grooming.
source: Thus, DNx01s may have a role beyond feedback control during grooming.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion.

claim: DNx01s may be used to respond to strong gusts of wind that initiate a stance stabilization reflex.
source: Because other DNs with large axons (e.g., giant fiber neurons) are often implicated in fast reflexive movements (King and Wyman, 1980; Azevedo et al., 2020), DNx01s may be used to respond to, for example, strong gusts of wind that initiate a stance stabilization reflex.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Other DNs with large axons (e.g., giant fiber neurons) are often implicated in fast reflexive movements.
source: Because other DNs with large axons (e.g., giant fiber neurons) are often implicated in fast reflexive movements (King and Wyman, 1980; Azevedo et al., 2020), DNx01s may be used to respond to, for example, strong gusts of wind that initiate a stance stabilization reflex.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to King and Wyman, 1980 and Azevedo et al., 2020.

claim: The SEZ is considered a center for action selection.
source: The SEZ is considered a center for action section (Mann et al., 2013; Tastekin et al., 2015) and is known to house numerous DNs (Namiki et al., 2018; Hsu and Bhandawat, 2016).
